title: Waves, Sound and Light
bigQuestion: How can a wiggle in a groove, a push of air or a beam of light carry a song, a voice or a picture across a room?

story.title: The Groove That Sings
story.kicker: Put a record under a magnifying glass and you can see sound before you hear it.
paragraphs: A black vinyl record spins on the turntable at 33 and one-third turns each minute. A thin needle rests in a groove that spirals from the outer edge toward the center. To the eye the groove looks like a smooth line. Put a magnifying glass over it and the line breaks apart. It wiggles. It swings left and right, sometimes in wide sweeps, sometimes in tiny jitters packed close together.

Those wiggles are not decoration. They are a drawing of sound. When the record was made, a singer's voice shook the air, the air shook a microphone, and a cutting tool carved every shake into a spiral. Now the needle rides the groove, shakes the same way, and turns each shake into a small electric signal. The speaker pushes the air, and the room hears a voice that was recorded decades ago.

Look closer and you can read the music. A loud drum hit makes the groove swing wide; a soft hum keeps it narrow. A high whistle makes tight, fast wiggles; a low bass note makes long, slow ones. Width and spacing are the two things that matter, and in this chapter they get names: amplitude and wavelength.

Sound, water ripples, a shaking rope and light all share this shape. They are waves, patterns that carry energy from one place to another without carrying the stuff itself. The needle does not travel to the singer. The groove stays on the record. Only the pattern moves, and the pattern is enough to bring the song back to life.
story.think: If you could see the groove for a whisper and the groove for a shout side by side, how would they look different, and why?

lessons.title: Energy Moves, the Stuff Stays
lessons.mainIdea: A wave carries energy from place to place, but the material it travels through only moves back and forth.
reading: Drop a pebble into a still pond. Rings spread out from the splash. A leaf floating nearby bobs up and down, but it does not ride the ring to the shore. It ends up almost where it started. The ring moved. The water and the leaf did not go with it. That is the strange and useful thing about a *wave*: the pattern travels, the material does not.

A wave is a repeating disturbance that carries *energy* from one place to another. Stretch a rope along the floor and snap one end up and down. A hump runs down the rope. Each piece of rope only rises and falls, yet the hump reaches the far end and can knock over a cup there. The rope stayed put; the energy arrived.

Sound works the same way. A drum skin pushes the air next to it. That air pushes the air next to it, and so on. The air near the drum never travels to your ear. It just shoves its neighbors. What reaches you is a chain of pushes, and your eardrum feels the energy of the last push in line. Scientists call the material a wave moves through the *medium*: water for ripples, rope for the hump, air for sound.

words.d: a repeating disturbance that carries energy from one place to another
the ability to make something move or change
the material a wave travels through, such as air, water or a rope

look.title: The Stadium Wave
look.text: Picture a crowd doing the wave at a Chicago ballpark. Each person stands up, throws their arms in the air, and sits back down. The wave races all the way around the stadium in about half a minute. Nobody leaves their seat.
look.prompt: What moved around the stadium, and what stayed put? How is this like a ripple on a pond?

check.q: A leaf floats on a pond when a ripple passes. What does the leaf do?
choices: Bobs up and down and stays near the same spot
Rides the ripple to the shore
Sinks because the wave pushes it under
check.why: A wave carries energy, not the water. The leaf rises and falls as the ripple passes but stays close to where it was.

check.q: What does a wave carry from one place to another?
check.why: A wave is a traveling pattern of energy. The medium moves back and forth in place while the energy travels through it.

check.q: A drum is hit across a gym. Which best describes how the sound reaches you?
choices: Air from the drum flies to your ear
The drum skin stretches across the gym
A chain of pushes passes from air to air until it reaches your ear
Your ear pulls the sound toward it
check.why: Each bit of air shoves its neighbor. The pushes travel across the room even though no single bit of air makes the trip.

lessons.title: Amplitude, Wavelength, Frequency
lessons.mainIdea: Amplitude tells how much energy a wave carries, wavelength is the distance between repeats, and frequency is how many repeats pass each second.
reading: Every wave can be measured in three ways. *Amplitude* is how far the medium moves from its rest position, the height of a water hump above the flat surface or how far a rope swings from the middle. Bigger amplitude means more energy. On the turntable, a loud drum hit cut a wide swing in the groove; a whisper cut a narrow one. Doubling the amplitude of a wave does not just double its energy. It roughly quadruples it, which is why a shout can rattle a window when a normal voice cannot.

*Wavelength* is the distance from one crest to the next crest, or from one groove wiggle to the next matching wiggle. Long ocean swells might be 100 meters from crest to crest. The ripples in a bathtub are a few centimeters. *Frequency* is a different measure: it counts how many complete waves pass a point in one second. The unit is the *hertz* (Hz). A rope shaken twice a second makes a 2 Hz wave.

Wavelength and frequency are linked. If the wave speed stays the same, more waves per second must be packed closer together. So high frequency goes with short wavelength, and low frequency goes with long wavelength. For sound, frequency is what we hear as pitch: a bass note is low frequency, a whistle is high. For the eye, amplitude shows up as brightness and frequency as color, an idea this chapter returns to later.

words.d: how far the medium moves from its rest position; larger amplitude means more energy
the distance from one crest of a wave to the next
the number of complete waves that pass a point each second
the unit of frequency; one hertz is one wave per second

look.title: Frequencies of Some Sounds
rows: Upper limit of young human hearing
look.prompt: Which of these sounds has the shortest wavelength in air? How do you know without measuring?

check.q: Which change to a wave would make it carry the most extra energy?
check.why: Amplitude measures how far the medium moves. More amplitude means more energy, and doubling it roughly quadruples the energy.

check.q: A rope is shaken so that 5 complete waves pass a point every second. What is the frequency?
check.why: Frequency counts complete waves per second, measured in hertz. Five waves each second is 5 Hz.

check.q: Two sound waves travel through the same air at the same speed. One has a higher frequency. What must be true?
check.why: At the same speed, more waves per second must fit closer together. Higher frequency means shorter wavelength. Loudness is a separate thing, amplitude.

lessons.title: Reading the Wave Bench
lessons.mainIdea: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength, so measuring any two of them tells you the third.
reading: The site's wave bench is a long tray of water with a paddle at one end. Set the paddle to move slowly and long, lazy ripples roll down the tray. Speed it up and the ripples get tighter and closer together, yet a marker floating in the tray shows each crest still takes the same time to travel the length of the bench. The speed of the ripples did not change. Only the spacing did.

This is a rule you can trust for any wave: *wave speed* equals frequency times wavelength. Say the paddle makes 2 waves per second and the crests are 0.5 meters apart. Then the crests travel 2 times 0.5, or 1 meter every second. Now double the frequency to 4 Hz. The water has not changed, so the speed is still 1 meter per second. That means the wavelength must shrink to 0.25 meters.

The rule matters because speed depends on the medium, not on the wave. Water of a certain depth carries ripples at one speed. Air at room temperature carries sound at one speed. So when a musician plays a higher note, the sound does not go faster; its wavelength gets shorter. On the turntable, the same idea appears as wiggles packed more tightly in the groove for the high notes, even though the record spins at a fixed rate.

You can use the rule on your own. Count how many ripples pass a mark in ten seconds, divide by ten to get frequency, then measure the crest-to-crest distance with a ruler. Multiply, and you have the wave speed of the bench without ever timing a single ripple.

words.d: how fast a crest travels through the medium; equal to frequency times wavelength
the highest point of a wave

look.title: Two Settings on the Paddle
look.text: On the wave bench, a student sets the paddle to 1 wave per second and measures the crests 30 centimeters apart. She then turns the paddle up to 3 waves per second. The water is the same depth. She measures again and finds the crests 10 centimeters apart.
look.prompt: What was the wave speed at each setting? What does that tell you about what controls wave speed?

check.q: A wave has a frequency of 4 Hz and a wavelength of 2 meters. How fast does it travel?
check.why: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength: 4 times 2 is 8 meters per second.

check.q: What mainly decides how fast a wave travels?
choices: How hard the source was hit
check.why: Speed depends on the medium. Changing the frequency changes the wavelength, not the speed, as long as the medium stays the same.

check.q: A flute plays a higher note. Compared with the lower note, the sound wave in the air has:
choices: A shorter wavelength and the same speed
A longer wavelength and a faster speed
The same wavelength and a faster speed
A shorter wavelength and a slower speed
check.why: The air is the same, so the speed is the same. A higher frequency must mean a shorter wavelength.

lessons.title: Sound Needs Something to Push
lessons.mainIdea: Sound is a mechanical wave: it travels only by pushing through a medium, so it cannot cross empty space.
reading: Around 1660 the English scientist Robert Boyle hung a ringing watch inside a glass jar and pumped the air out. As the air thinned, the ticking faded. With most of the air gone, he could see the watch working but could not hear it. Let the air back in and the sound returned. Boyle had shown that sound needs a *medium*. Nothing in the jar was able to carry the pushes to the glass.

Sound is a *mechanical wave*, a wave that moves by shoving particles of matter into each other. A vibrating guitar string squeezes the air on one side, then the other, hundreds of times each second. Each squeeze is a region of slightly higher pressure, and each pull-back is a region of slightly lower pressure. These squeezes travel outward as a *compression* wave. In a *vacuum*, a space with no particles, there is nothing to squeeze, and sound simply stops.

This is why films that show roaring explosions in space are wrong. An astronaut outside the International Space Station hears nothing through the vacuum. Inside a suit, a radio carries voices, because radio is not sound. It is a different kind of wave, one that needs no medium, and it is the subject of the next section.

You can feel the medium at work on the site's drum bench. Tap a drum and hold a hand a few centimeters from the skin. You feel the puffs of air. Rest a fingertip on the skin instead and the sound dies, because you stopped the vibration that was doing the pushing.

words.d: a wave that travels by pushing particles of a medium against each other; sound is one
a region in a sound wave where particles are squeezed closer together
a space with no matter in it, not even air

look.title: Boyle's Bell in the Jar
look.text: In his reports on the air pump, Boyle described placing a watch or small bell inside the glass receiver and pumping the air out. As the air was removed, the sound grew faint until it could scarcely be heard, though the mechanism could still be seen moving. When air was let back in, the sound returned.
look.cite: Robert Boyle, experiments with the air pump, about 1660
look.prompt: Why did Boyle need to see the watch still working? What would he have concluded if he had not checked?

check.q: Why does a ringing bell go silent inside a jar with the air pumped out?
choices: The bell stops vibrating in a vacuum
There are no particles to carry the pushes to the glass
check.why: Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a medium. With no air, the vibrations of the bell have nothing to push on.

check.q: Which of these could an astronaut floating outside a spacecraft hear directly through space?
choices: Nothing, because space is a vacuum
check.why: Space has almost no particles, so sound cannot travel through it at any loudness. Radio works because it is not sound.

check.q: What is a compression in a sound wave?
choices: A place where the medium is missing
A place where the wave stops
A place where particles are spread apart
A place where particles are squeezed closer together
check.why: A vibrating object squeezes the air in front of it. That squeezed region, the compression, travels outward as part of the wave.

lessons.title: How Fast Sound Travels
lessons.mainIdea: Sound moves at about 343 meters per second in air, faster in water, and faster still in steel, because stiffer, denser media pass pushes along more quickly.
reading: Watch a lightning flash and start counting. Thunder arrives a few seconds later. The light reached you almost instantly, but the sound crawled along at about 343 meters per second, the *speed of sound* in air at room temperature. Every 3 seconds of delay means the strike was roughly 1 kilometer away. Sound is fast by human standards, but the flash shows you it is not instant.

The speed of sound depends on the medium. In water, sound travels about 1,480 meters per second, more than four times faster than in air. In steel, it races along at nearly 6,000 meters per second. Particles in liquids and solids are packed closer and bonded more stiffly, so a push at one end is passed to the far end quickly. Air particles are far apart and must fly across gaps before they bump the next one.

This is why a swimmer hears a clank underwater before a friend on the dock does. It is also why old stories tell of people pressing an ear to a rail to hear a distant train. Temperature matters too. Warm air carries sound a little faster than cold air. Its particles are already moving faster, so they pass the push along sooner.

words.d: how fast a sound wave travels through a medium; about 343 m/s in air at room temperature
one of the tiny pieces, such as atoms or molecules, that make up matter

look.title: Speed of Sound in Different Media
look.prompt: Why might a sound cross a swimming pool faster than it crosses a gym of the same length?

check.q: You see lightning and hear thunder 6 seconds later. About how far away was the strike?
check.why: Sound covers about 343 meters each second, so 3 seconds is roughly 1 kilometer and 6 seconds is roughly 2 kilometers.

check.q: In which medium does sound travel fastest?
check.why: Steel particles are tightly packed and stiffly bonded, so they pass each push along quickly. Sound does not travel in a vacuum at all.

check.q: Why does sound travel faster in water than in air?
choices: Sound waves are bigger in water
Water particles are closer together and pass pushes along faster
check.why: In a liquid the particles are packed close and each push reaches the next particle sooner. In air, particles must cross gaps first.

lessons.title: How the Ear Hears
lessons.mainIdea: The ear turns air pressure waves into vibrations of the eardrum, then into nerve signals inside the cochlea.
reading: A sound wave that reaches your head is a train of tiny pressure changes in the air. The outer ear funnels them down a short canal to the *eardrum*, a thin skin about the size of a fingernail. Each compression pushes the eardrum in; each stretch lets it spring out. The eardrum vibrates at the same frequency as the sound, thousands of times a second for a high note.

Behind the eardrum sit three tiny bones, the smallest in the body. They work like a lever, passing the vibration to a snail-shaped tube called the *cochlea*, which is filled with fluid. Inside, thousands of hair cells sit along a membrane that is stiff at one end and floppy at the other. High-frequency vibrations shake the stiff end, low ones the far end. Each hair cell fires a nerve signal when its part of the membrane moves, so the brain learns the pitch from which cells are firing.

Loudness is measured in *decibels* (dB). A whisper is about 30 dB, normal talk about 60 dB, and a loud concert can pass 110 dB. Very loud sound bends the hair cells too far and can break them. Unlike skin, they do not grow back. That is why hearing protection matters near power tools and why doctors warn about turning earbuds all the way up.

words.d: a thin membrane in the ear that vibrates when sound waves hit it
a snail-shaped, fluid-filled tube in the inner ear where vibrations become nerve signals
the unit used to measure how loud a sound is

look.title: How Loud Is It?
look.cite: approximate values, NIOSH and CDC hearing-safety materials
look.prompt: Where on this list do you think hearing damage becomes possible after long exposure? What could a worker do about it?

check.q: What does the eardrum do when a sound wave reaches it?
choices: It absorbs the sound and turns it into heat
It sends the sound wave back out of the ear
It stays still while the bones move
It vibrates at the same frequency as the sound
check.why: The pressure changes in the wave push and release the eardrum, so it vibrates in step with the sound.

check.q: How does the brain tell a high note from a low note?
choices: Different hair cells along the cochlea fire for different frequencies
The eardrum vibrates louder for high notes
The three bones move only for low notes
The outer ear folds change shape
check.why: The membrane in the cochlea responds to high frequencies near one end and low frequencies near the other. Which hair cells fire tells the brain the pitch.

check.q: Why can very loud sound cause permanent hearing loss?
choices: Hair cells in the cochlea can break and do not regrow
Loud sound travels faster and skips the ear
check.why: Loud sounds bend the hair cells too far. Broken hair cells are not replaced, so the loss can be permanent.

lessons.title: Light Needs No Medium
lessons.mainIdea: Light is a wave that can cross empty space and travels about 300,000 kilometers per second, far faster than sound.
reading: Sunlight crosses about 150 million kilometers of nearly empty space to reach Earth. Sound could never make that trip; it needs particles to push. Light does not. It is an *electromagnetic wave*, a traveling pattern of electric and magnetic fields that carries its own energy along without a medium. In empty space it moves at about 300,000 kilometers per second, the fastest anything can travel.

That speed is so great that light seems instant on Earth. Flip a switch and the room is lit with no delay you can notice. But over big distances the delay shows. Light from the sun takes about 8 minutes to reach us. When you look at the moon, you see it as it was a little over a second ago. The first person to measure this delay was the Danish astronomer Ole Roemer in 1676, who noticed that the eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io ran late when Earth was far from Jupiter and early when it was close.

Light is still a wave, with amplitude, wavelength and frequency. Amplitude shows up as brightness. Wavelength and frequency show up as color. Red light has the longest wavelength the eye can see, about 700 nanometers, and violet the shortest, about 400. A nanometer is one billionth of a meter, so several hundred waves of visible light fit across the width of a single human hair.

words.d: a wave of electric and magnetic fields that carries energy and needs no medium; light is one
one billionth of a meter, used to measure wavelengths of light

look.title: Roemer and the Late Eclipses
look.text: Roemer reported to the French Academy that the moments when Jupiter's moon Io vanished into the planet's shadow did not keep a steady schedule. When Earth was moving away from Jupiter the eclipses came later than predicted, and when Earth was approaching they came earlier. He argued that the difference was the time light needed to cross the extra distance, and that light therefore travels at a finite speed.
look.cite: Ole Roemer, report to the Académie des Sciences, Paris, 1676
look.prompt: Why would eclipses of a moon of Jupiter be a good clock for testing whether light takes time to travel?

check.q: Why can light from the sun reach Earth when sound from the sun cannot?
choices: Light needs no medium; sound cannot cross the near-vacuum of space
Sound is absorbed by the moon
check.why: Light is an electromagnetic wave and carries itself through empty space. Sound is mechanical and needs particles, which space mostly lacks.

check.q: About how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
check.why: Light covers about 300,000 kilometers each second. The 150 million kilometers to the sun take about 8 minutes.

check.q: For light, what does a change in wavelength show up as to the eye?
check.why: Wavelength and frequency set the color of light. Amplitude sets brightness. Loudness belongs to sound, not light.

lessons.title: Bounce, Soak, Pass Through
lessons.mainIdea: When light meets a material it can reflect, be absorbed, or be transmitted, and the mix decides what we see.
reading: Stand in a sunny room and look around. The mirror shows your face. The black sweater on the chair looks dark and feels warm. The window lets the yard show through. Each object is doing something different with the same sunlight. Light can *reflect*, bouncing off a surface. It can be *absorbed*, its energy taken in and usually turned into heat. Or it can be *transmitted*, passing through. Most objects do a mix of all three.

Reflection follows a simple rule. Light bounces off a smooth surface at the same angle it came in, like a ball off a wall. A mirror is smooth enough to keep the rays in order, so an image forms. A sheet of white paper reflects almost as much light as a mirror. But its surface is bumpy at a tiny scale, so the rays scatter in every direction. That is why paper looks bright but shows no image.

Color comes from which wavelengths get absorbed. A red apple absorbs most of the blue and green in white light and reflects the red. A black shirt absorbs nearly all colors, which is why it warms up faster in sunlight than a white one. A clear window transmits most light, while tinted glass absorbs some wavelengths and transmits the rest. On a hot Chicago afternoon, that is the difference between a car with a black roof and one with a white roof.

words.d: to bounce off a surface
to take in light energy, usually turning it into heat
to let light pass through

look.title: Two Cars in the Sun
look.text: Two cars sit in a parking lot in July. One is black, the other white. After an hour, a student rests a hand on each roof. The black roof is too hot to touch. The white roof is warm but bearable. Both were parked at the same time in the same sun.
look.prompt: Explain the difference using the words reflect and absorb. What color would you choose for a roof in a hot city, and why?

check.q: Why does white paper look bright but not show your reflection like a mirror?
choices: Paper reflects light but scatters it in every direction
Paper transmits the light to the other side
check.why: Paper reflects a lot of light, but its rough surface sends rays off in all directions, so no ordered image forms.

check.q: A green leaf looks green because it:
choices: Reflects green light and absorbs most other colors
check.why: The color we see is the light that comes back to our eyes. The leaf reflects green and absorbs most of the red and blue.

check.q: Which object transmits the most light?
check.why: Transmit means to let light pass through. A clear window does this best. A mirror reflects and a black sweater absorbs.

lessons.title: Refraction: Light Bends
lessons.mainIdea: Light changes speed when it enters a new material, and that change of speed bends its path.
reading: Put a pencil in a glass of water and look from the side. The pencil seems to break at the surface. Nothing happened to the pencil. The light coming from the underwater part bent as it left the water and entered the air. This bending is called *refraction*, and it happens whenever light crosses from one material into another at an angle.

The cause is speed. Light travels slower in water than in air, and slower still in glass. When a beam hits the surface at a slant, one edge of the beam enters the slow material first and is held back while the other edge is still moving fast. The beam swings around, the way a line of marching students turns if the ones on one end slow down. Light entering a slower material bends toward the line straight into the surface; light leaving it bends away.

Refraction is everywhere. It makes a swimming pool look shallower than it is. It splits white light into a rainbow when it passes through a prism, because each color slows by a slightly different amount and so bends by a slightly different angle. Isaac Newton showed this with a prism in a darkened room in the 1660s. And refraction is the whole trick behind a lens, the subject of the next section.

words.d: the bending of light as it passes from one material into another
a wedge of glass that spreads white light into its colors

look.title: Speed of Light in Different Materials
look.prompt: In which material would light bend the most when entering from air? Why is diamond so sparkly compared with glass?

check.q: A pencil in a glass of water looks bent because:
choices: Light bends as it passes from water into air
Light is absorbed by the water
check.why: Light from the underwater part of the pencil changes speed and direction at the surface, so the image appears shifted.

check.q: What is the direct cause of refraction?
choices: Light changes speed when it enters a new material
Light changes color when it enters a new material
check.why: Light slows down or speeds up when it crosses into a new medium. At an angle, that speed change turns the beam.

check.q: Why does a prism separate white light into colors?
choices: The prism adds color to the light
Each color slows by a different amount and bends by a different angle
The prism reflects each color from a different face
check.why: White light contains all the colors. Each wavelength refracts slightly differently in glass, so they spread apart.

lessons.title: The Eye Is a Camera
lessons.mainIdea: The eye's cornea and lens refract light to form an image on the retina, where cells turn light into nerve signals.
reading: Your eye is a ball about 2.4 centimeters across with a window in the front. Light enters through the clear *cornea*, which does most of the bending. Then it passes through the *pupil*, the dark hole in the middle. The pupil widens in dim light and shrinks in bright light. Behind the pupil sits the *lens*, a soft, clear disc that fine-tunes the focus. Together the cornea and lens refract the rays so they meet on the back wall of the eye.

That back wall is the *retina*, a thin layer of light-sensing cells. The image that lands there is upside down and backward, just as in a camera, but the brain flips it without your noticing. Two kinds of cells do the sensing. Rods work in dim light and see only shades of gray. Cones need brighter light and come in three types tuned to different wavelengths, roughly red, green and blue. Mixing their signals gives every color you see.

The lens can change shape. Small muscles around it squeeze it thicker to focus on a near page and let it flatten to focus on a distant sign. That is why your eyes feel tired after a long time reading up close: the muscles have been working the whole time. With age the lens stiffens, which is why many adults past 40 start holding menus at arm's length.

words.d: the clear front surface of the eye that bends most of the incoming light
the opening in the eye that lets light in; it changes size with brightness
a clear, curved piece of material that bends light to focus it
the layer of light-sensing cells at the back of the eye

look.title: From Bright Sun to a Dark Hallway
look.text: A student walks in from a bright sidewalk into a dim school hallway. For a few seconds she can barely see. Then shapes appear, then faces. Later, walking back outside, the sunlight feels painfully bright until her eyes adjust again.
look.prompt: Which part of the eye is changing during those seconds, and why does the change take time in each direction?

check.q: Which part of the eye does most of the bending of incoming light?
check.why: The clear cornea at the front does most of the refraction. The lens behind it fine-tunes the focus.

check.q: What is the image on the retina like compared with the scene?
check.why: Like a camera, the eye's lens forms an inverted image. The brain corrects it so the world looks upright.

check.q: Why do colors fade in very dim light?
choices: Cones need bright light, so only the rods, which see gray, are working
Light has no color in the dark
check.why: Cone cells sense color but need more light. In dim light the rods take over, and rods report only brightness.

lessons.title: Glasses Fix the Focus
lessons.mainIdea: Nearsighted and farsighted eyes focus light in the wrong place, and a lens of the right shape moves the focus onto the retina.
reading: Some eyes are a little too long from front to back. Light from distant objects comes to a focus before it reaches the retina, then spreads out again, so the far-away sign is a blur while a nearby book is sharp. This is *nearsightedness*, and it is common in teenagers. The fix is a *concave* lens, thinner in the middle than at the edges. It spreads the rays slightly apart before they enter the eye, so they meet a little farther back, right on the retina.

Other eyes are a little too short, or their lens has stiffened with age. Light from a near object would come to a focus behind the retina if it could, so the page is blurry while the far sign is clear. This is *farsightedness*. The fix is a *convex* lens, thicker in the middle, which bends the rays inward so they meet sooner. Reading glasses sold at a drugstore are simple convex lenses.

An eye doctor finds the right lens by trial. You look at letters through lens after lens until the blur snaps into focus, and the strength of that lens is written on your prescription. Contact lenses do the same job by sitting directly on the cornea. Laser surgery reshapes the cornea itself to change how strongly it refracts. All three are the same idea: move the focus onto the retina.

words.d: a condition where distant objects look blurry because light focuses in front of the retina
a condition where near objects look blurry because light would focus behind the retina
a lens thinner in the middle than at the edges; it spreads light rays apart
a lens thicker in the middle than at the edges; it brings light rays together

look.title: Back Row, Front Row
look.text: A student in the back row of a classroom in Rockford keeps squinting at the board but reads her worksheet easily. Her grandfather holds the newspaper far from his face and says the print is too small, though he can read street signs across the road.
look.prompt: Which of them is nearsighted and which is farsighted? What shape of lens would help each one, and why?

check.q: In a nearsighted eye, where does light from a distant object come to a focus?
check.why: The eye is slightly too long, so rays meet before the retina and spread out again, blurring distant objects.

check.q: Which lens helps a farsighted person read a book?
check.why: A convex lens brings rays together sooner, moving the focus forward onto the retina.

check.q: A concave lens is used for nearsightedness because it:
choices: Spreads rays apart so they focus farther back
Bends rays inward so they focus sooner
check.why: Spreading the rays slightly apart before they enter the eye pushes the focus back onto the retina.

review.q: A cork floats on a pond as ripples pass. Which statement is true?
choices: The cork travels with the ripples to the shore
The water carries the cork forward one wavelength per ripple
The ripples stop at the cork
The cork bobs in place while energy passes by
review.why: Waves carry energy, not the medium. The cork stays roughly in place and moves up and down.

review.q: Which describes the sound of a loud, low bass note?
review.why: Loud means large amplitude. Low pitch means low frequency and long wavelength.

review.q: A wave on the bench has a frequency of 2 Hz and a wavelength of 0.4 m. Its speed is:
review.why: Speed equals frequency times wavelength: 2 times 0.4 is 0.8 meters per second.

review.q: Which wave can travel through the vacuum of space?
review.why: Light is electromagnetic and needs no medium. The others are mechanical waves and need matter to push.

review.q: You hear thunder 9 seconds after a lightning flash. The strike was about:
review.why: Sound travels about 343 meters per second, so about 1 kilometer every 3 seconds. Nine seconds is about 3 kilometers.

review.q: In the ear, where are vibrations turned into nerve signals?
review.why: Hair cells inside the fluid-filled cochlea fire nerve signals when their part of the membrane moves.

review.q: A blue shirt looks blue in sunlight because it:
choices: Reflects blue light and absorbs the other colors
review.why: The color you see is the light the object sends back. The shirt reflects blue and absorbs most of the rest.

review.q: A student cannot read the board from the back of the room but reads a book fine. Which lens will help?
review.why: She is nearsighted: light focuses in front of the retina. A concave lens spreads the rays so they focus farther back, on the retina.
